pages.text: Maaya pressed her face to the bus window. The sea flashed blue between the palm trees, and then a huge white fort rose up beside the road. “That is Elmina Castle,” said Madam Ankrah. “It is one of the oldest European buildings outside Europe. Today we find out why it was built here, and what it became.”

The sea flashed blue between the palm trees, and then a huge white fort rose up beside the road.
“That is Elmina Castle,” said Madam Ankrah.
“It is one of the oldest European buildings outside Europe.
Today we find out why it was built here, and what it became.”
pages.alt: A school bus drives past a large white fort beside the blue sea.

pages.text: In the courtyard, Madam Ankrah showed them a map. “In 1471, Portuguese sailors reached this coast,” she said. “They heard about gold, and they came back to trade for it. People here already had gold and already knew how to trade. The Portuguese king decided to build a fort to protect his ships and his trade.”

People here already had gold and already knew how to trade.
The Portuguese king decided to build a fort to protect his ships and his trade.”
pages.alt: A teacher points to a map of the coast while pupils look on.

pages.text: “Their fleet arrived on 19 January 1482,” said Madam Ankrah. “Building began the next morning. A captain named Diogo de Azambuja led the fleet, and King John II of Portugal gave the order. They named it São Jorge da Mina, which means Saint George of the Mine. The town that grew beside it became known as Elmina.”

A captain named Diogo de Azambuja led the fleet, and King John II of Portugal gave the order.
They named it São Jorge da Mina, which means Saint George of the Mine.
The town that grew beside it became known as Elmina.”
pages.alt: A drawing of ships landing and workers unloading stone near a rocky shore.

pages.text: “So it was a shop with walls,” said Paa. “Partly,” said Madam Ankrah. “It stored trade goods and guarded them from rival European ships. Cloth and other goods came in, and gold went out. Then, over time, something else was traded here: people. Enslaved men, women and children were bought and sold. That is the hardest part of this story.”

Then, over time, something else was traded here: people.
Enslaved men, women and children were bought and sold.
That is the hardest part of this story.”
pages.alt: Two pupils listen quietly as the teacher speaks with a serious face.

pages.text: “In 1637, Dutch forces captured the castle from the Portuguese,” said Madam Ankrah. “They had tried once before, in 1596, and failed. Under the Dutch, the castle was used to hold enslaved Africans before ships carried them across the Atlantic. The Dutch trade in enslaved people went on until 1814.” Maaya wrote the dates down carefully and underlined 1637.

pages.text: “Not every date is easy,” said Madam Ankrah. “Most books say the Dutch took the castle in 1637, but some give 1642 for the end of the whole Portuguese Gold Coast. And some historians think a young Christopher Columbus may have sailed on a Portuguese voyage in 1481. Others doubt it. When experts disagree, we say so.” Paa grinned. “Even castles have mysteries.”

pages.alt: A chart with three question marks beside the dates 1637, 1642 and 1481.

pages.text: In the evening light, the guide spoke to the class. “In 1979, UNESCO listed this castle and other forts and castles along our coast as World Heritage Sites,” he said. “Today Elmina Castle is a museum run by Ghanaians. We do not keep it because the trade was good. We keep it so that nobody forgets what happened, and so that everyone can learn the truth.”

pages.text: On the bus home, Maaya did a sum. “2026 take away 1482 is 544 years,” she said. “Five hundred and forty-four years, and the walls are still here.” “Then it is our job to tell the story truthfully,” said Paa. Madam Ankrah smiled. “That is what history is for.” The end.

activities.question: Why did the Portuguese king order the fort to be built?
options: To protect his ships and the trade in gold

activities.prompt: The castle changed hands over time. What do you think happened to the people who ran it?
options: Different European powers took turns controlling it
The same people ran it for ever

activities.question: What does Madam Ankrah say we should do when experts disagree?
options: Pick the date we like best

activities.definition: A person or group that competes with another.

activities.prompt: Put the Elmina Castle story in order.
items: Portuguese sailors reached the coast in 1471.
Building of the castle began in January 1482.
Dutch forces captured the castle in 1637.

activities.prompt: Some history is hard to hear. How can we learn about painful things with respect?

Forced to work for others without freedom or pay.
